splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for the thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date, allowing more current data to inform calculations.

circuits.name: Sixth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the judgment's specified time when a person absconds. The outcome affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, extending the court's jurisdiction to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled by absconding because there is no statutory basis for the doctrine, and courts lack authority to extend punishment beyond what the statute provides.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prevents relitigating any previously presented claim — in addition to § 2255(h)'s separate gatekeeping requirements. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are more strictly constrained in successive collateral attacks than Congress may have intended.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar on relitigating previously raised claims under § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing a strict gatekeeping requirement.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar does not apply to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, who need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to state voting rules. Some circuits grant candidates standing based on competitive injury, while others require a more concrete showing of harm. The outcome affects whether election-procedure disputes can be resolved before or only after elections.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules that allegedly dilute lawful votes or alter election outcomes, based on competitive injury.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election absent a concrete showing that the challenged law will cause them personal and particularized injury.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps deference to Sentencing Commission commentary (Kisor/Auer deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions of the Sentencing Guidelines in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the interaction between the rule of lenity and agency deference in interpreting the Sentencing Guidelines. At least three circuits hold that lenity trumps deference, while the Third Circuit has held that deference can override lenity. This split affects how ambiguous sentencing enhancements are resolved and has implications for defendants' sentences nationwide.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency (Sentencing Commission) interpretations when construing ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary can override the rule of lenity, allowing anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions to control.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any single criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) (conjunctive reading) or if possessing any one criterion is disqualifying (disjunctive reading). This directly affects mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses across the country.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they satisfy all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any single criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or.'

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is a valid and authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline after Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary adding inchoate offenses (conspiracy, aiding and abetting, attempt) to the definition of 'controlled substance offense' in the career-offender guideline is entitled to deference. Some circuits defer to the commentary under Stinson, while others hold it impermissibly expands the unambiguous guideline text. This affects whether defendants convicted of drug conspiracy qualify as career offenders.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and controlling
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1's inclusion of inchoate offenses in the definition of 'controlled substance offense' is a valid interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and entitled to controlling weight under Stinson/Kisor.

positions.label: Commentary is invalid — guideline text is unambiguous
positions.summary: Holds that the text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance underlying a state conviction to also be controlled under federal law, or whether any substance controlled under state law qualifies.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a state drug conviction counts as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines even if the substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act. This matters for career-offender and base-offense-level enhancements, particularly for substances like certain marijuana analogues controlled only by states.

positions.label: No federal-law match required
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses regardless of whether the substance is federally scheduled, finding no textual basis to graft a federal limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Federal-law match required
positions.summary: Holds that a state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines only if the substance at issue is also controlled under federal law.

circuits.name: First Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. De La Rosa

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in law can be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release. Some circuits categorically exclude such changes, while others, bolstered by the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6), permit courts to consider them. This affects thousands of prisoners serving sentences under outdated mandatory minimums.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, and the Sentencing Commission's attempt to say otherwise exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive sentencing changes can be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement in U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6).

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the deadline to appeal a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil appeal deadline (30 days) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal proceeding (triggering the 30-day civil deadline) or a criminal matter (triggering the 14-day criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies (30 days)
positions.summary: Holds that the Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Ranger Elec. Commc'ns

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies (14 days)
positions.summary: Holds that the Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case and therefore the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner's challenge to BOP decisions regarding conditions or terms of confinement (such as transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act) must be brought as a habeas petition under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 or may be brought as a civil rights action.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to conditions or terms of confinement that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment must be brought exclusively through habeas corpus or may proceed as civil rights actions. This affects prisoners' access to remedies and the procedural requirements they must satisfy, including exhaustion and the Prison Litigation Reform Act.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for duration-related claims
positions.summary: Holds that claims seeking earlier release or transfer to prerelease custody challenge the duration of confinement and must be brought through habeas corpus under § 2241, not through civil rights statutes.

positions.label: Civil rights actions may also be available
positions.summary: Holds that some challenges to BOP decisions about conditions or terms of confinement may proceed as civil rights actions rather than exclusively through habeas, particularly when they do not directly challenge the fact of imprisonment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's property belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value during a Chapter 13 case becomes part of the bankruptcy estate upon conversion to Chapter 7. This affects whether debtors can retain equity growth in their homes and other assets when they convert, with significant consequences for debtor protections in bankruptcy.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity belong to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, based on the broad scope of 'property of the estate' under § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtor, not the estate, consistent with the statute's structure, legislative history, and policy of protecting good-faith converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant for the conduct underlying a supervised release violation, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of the court's trust.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly impose punishment at revocation for the violating conduct itself, placing it at the extreme end of a circuit split. Other circuits hold that revocation sentences should be based on the breach of the supervisory relationship, not as punishment for the new offense. This affects how district courts explain and justify revocation sentences.

positions.label: Courts may punish for underlying violation conduct
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences as punishment for the conduct that violated supervised release, not just for the breach of trust.

positions.label: Revocation should address breach of trust, not punish new conduct
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release revocation is fundamentally about sanctioning the breach of the court's trust, and revocation sentences should not be imposed as punishment for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denials of motions to seal medical records qualify for immediate appeal under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order.' Other circuits have not uniformly recognized this category as satisfying the collateral order doctrine, creating uncertainty about when litigants can immediately appeal sealing denials.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denials of motions to seal medical records are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal — even those involving sensitive medical information — are generally not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because they can be reviewed after final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted cert to resolve disagreements about the legal standards for discrimination claims in business or hospitality settings. The grant indicates the Second Circuit's approach was sufficiently important or unsettled to warrant review, suggesting a circuit split on liability standards and available remedies.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied legal standards for discrimination in hospitality settings that the Supreme Court found sufficiently questionable to grant certiorari for review.

positions.label: Conflicting approach
positions.summary: Other circuits have applied different standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business or hospitality establishments, creating the disagreement that prompted SCOTUS review.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
